metadata.title: On Weak Chromatic Polynomials of Mixed Graphs

extraction_notes.note: One align environment carries both numbered equations (1) and (2); emitted as a single equation node with the fact's span, so both \ref keys resolve to EP1.
The parenthetical sentence extending the notation $u \rightarrow v$ to arcs is kept inside the orientation definition rather than as a separate notation node.
The reduction procedure for computing weak chromatic polynomials is described in prose; extracted as an unmarked algorithm whose steps split the second sentence at 'until'.

Proposition 6 is justified only by 'The standard proof ... gives:', taken as a zero-step prose proof (PrP1 rigor semi_formal). The lead-in 'Propositions 6 and 7 give the following equations:' sits outside any node, so its two dependencies were added by hand.

nodes.name: Mixed graph
nodes.statement: A \emph{mixed graph} $G = (V, E, A)$ consists of a set of vertices, $V=V(G)$, a set of undirected edges, $E=E(G)$, and a set of directed edges, $A=A(G)$.

nodes.name: Edges and arcs
nodes.statement: For convenience, the elements of $E$ will be called \emph{edges} and the elements of $A$ will be called \emph{arcs}.

nodes.name: Edge and arc notation $uv$, $\vec{uv}$
nodes.statement: Given adjacent vertices $u,v \in V$, an edge will be denoted by $uv$ and an arc will be denoted by $\vec{uv}$.

nodes.name: $k$-coloring
nodes.statement: A \emph{$k$-coloring} of a mixed graph $G$ is a mapping $c: V \rightarrow [k]$, where $[k] := \{1, 2, \ldots, k\}$.

nodes.name: Weak and strong proper $k$-coloring
nodes.statement: A \emph{weak} (resp.\ \emph{strong}) \emph{proper $k$-coloring} of $G$ is a $k$-coloring such that \[ c(u) \neq c(v) \ \text{ if } uv \in E \qquad \text{ and } \qquad c(u) \le c(v) \ \text{ (resp. $c(u) < c(v)$) \ if } \vec{uv} \in A \, . \]
nodes.statement_short: A $k$-coloring is weakly proper if edge endpoints get different colors and arcs are weakly increasing (strictly, for strong).

nodes.name: Weak and strong chromatic polynomial
nodes.statement: The \emph{weak} (resp.\ \emph{strong}) \emph{chromatic polynomial}, denoted by $\chi_G(k)$ (resp.\ $\widehat{\chi}_G(k)$), is the number of weak (resp. strong) proper $k$-colorings of $G$.
nodes.statement_short: $\chi_G(k)$ (resp. $\widehat{\chi}_G(k)$) counts weak (resp. strong) proper $k$-colorings of $G$.

nodes.name: Polynomiality of mixed-graph chromatic functions
nodes.statement: It is well known (see, e.g., \cite{kotekmakowskyzilber,sotskovtanaev}) that these counting functions are indeed polynomials in $k$.
conclusions: these counting functions are indeed polynomials in $k$

nodes.name: Orientation of a mixed graph
nodes.statement: An \emph{orientation} of a mixed graph $G$ is obtained by orienting the edges of $G$, i.e., assigning one of $u$ and $v$ to be the head/tail of the edge $uv \in E$; if $v$ is the head we use the notation $u \to v$. (An arc $\vec{uv}$, for which we also use the notation $u \rightarrow v$, cannot be re-oriented.)
differentia: obtained by orienting the edges of $G$
nodes.statement_short: An orientation assigns a head and tail to every undirected edge; arcs keep their direction; $u \to v$ denotes the result.

nodes.name: Acyclic orientation
nodes.statement: An orientation of a mixed graph is \emph{acyclic} if it does not contain any directed cycles.
differentia: it does not contain any directed cycles

nodes.name: Acyclic mixed graph
nodes.statement: A mixed graph is \emph{acyclic} if all of its possible orientations are acyclic.
differentia: all of its possible orientations are acyclic

nodes.name: Compatible coloring and orientation
nodes.statement: A coloring $c$ and an orientation of $G$ are \emph{compatible} if for every $u \to v$ in the orientation, $c(u) \le c(v)$.

nodes.name: Stanley's reciprocity theorem for chromatic polynomials
nodes.statement: A famous theorem of Stanley says that, for any graph $G=(V,E,\varnothing)$ and positive integer $k$, $(-1)^{|V|} \chi_G(-k)$ enumerates the pairs of $k$-colorings and compatible acyclic orientations of $G$ and, in particular, $(-1)^{|V|} \chi_G(-1)$ equals the number of acyclic orientations of $G$ \cite{stanleyacyclic}; this is an example of a \emph{combinatorial reciprocity theorem}.
assumptions: for any graph $G=(V,E,\varnothing)$ and positive integer $k$
conclusions: $(-1)^{|V|} \chi_G(-k)$ enumerates the pairs of $k$-colorings and compatible acyclic orientations of $G$
in particular, $(-1)^{|V|} \chi_G(-1)$ equals the number of acyclic orientations of $G$
nodes.statement_short: $(-1)^{|V|}\chi_G(-k)$ counts pairs of $k$-colorings and compatible acyclic orientations of a graph $G$.

nodes.name: Reciprocity theorem for strong chromatic polynomials of mixed graphs
nodes.statement: For any mixed graph $G=(V,E,A)$ and positive integer $k$, $(-1)^{|V|} \widehat{\chi}_G(-k)$ equals the number of $k$-colorings of $G$, each counted with multiplicity equal to the number of compatible acyclic orientations of~$G$.
assumptions: For any mixed graph $G=(V,E,A)$ and positive integer $k$
conclusions: $(-1)^{|V|} \widehat{\chi}_G(-k)$ equals the number of $k$-colorings of $G$, each counted with multiplicity equal to the number of compatible acyclic orientations of~$G$
nodes.statement_short: $(-1)^{|V|}\widehat{\chi}_G(-k)$ counts $k$-colorings weighted by their numbers of compatible acyclic orientations.
nodes.label: strongmg

nodes.name: Intercompatible coloring and orientation
nodes.statement: A coloring $c$ and an orientation of $G$ are \emph{intercompatible} if for every $u \to v$ in the orientation, \[ c(u) \le c(v) \ \text{ if } uv \in E(G) \qquad \text{ and } \qquad c(u)<c(v) \ \text{ if } \vec{uv} \in A(G) \, . \]
nodes.statement_short: A coloring and orientation are intercompatible if oriented edges weakly increase and arcs strictly increase in color.

nodes.name: Reciprocity theorem for weak chromatic polynomials of mixed graphs
nodes.statement: For any acyclic mixed graph $G=(V,E,A)$ and positive integer $k$, $(-1)^{|V|} {\chi}_G(-k)$ equals the number of $k$-colorings of $G$, each counted with multiplicity equal to the number of intercompatible acyclic orientations of~$G$.
assumptions: For any acyclic mixed graph $G=(V,E,A)$ and positive integer $k$
conclusions: $(-1)^{|V|} {\chi}_G(-k)$ equals the number of $k$-colorings of $G$, each counted with multiplicity equal to the number of intercompatible acyclic orientations of~$G$
nodes.statement_short: For acyclic mixed $G$, $(-1)^{|V|}\chi_G(-k)$ counts $k$-colorings weighted by their numbers of intercompatible acyclic orientations.
nodes.label: main

nodes.name: Acyclicity is needed for weak reciprocity
nodes.statement: One can prove this theorem along somewhat similar lines to the (geometric) approach used in \cite{Golomb}, though there are subtle details that distinguish the case of weak chromatic polynomials from the one of strong chromatic polynomials. For example, although both Theorems \ref{strongmg} and \ref{main} result in relating $k$-colorings of a mixed graph to its acyclic orientations, the reciprocity theorem for strong chromatic polynomials applies to all mixed graphs $G$, while the reciprocity theorem for weak chromatic polynomials requires the condition that $G$ be an acyclic mixed graph: without this condition, Theorem \ref{main} is not true.
nodes.statement_short: The weak reciprocity theorem, unlike the strong one, needs $G$ to be an acyclic mixed graph; it fails otherwise.

nodes.name: Poset
nodes.statement: Recall that a partially ordered set (a \emph{poset}) is a set $P$ with a relation $\preceq$ that is reflexive, antisymmetric, and transitive.
nodes.section: 2 Posets, Order Polynomials, and the Proof of Theorem 2

nodes.name: $\omega$-labeling and order polynomial
nodes.statement: Following \cite{stanleythesis} (see also \cite[Chapter 3]{Stanley}), we define an \emph{$\omega$-labeling} of a poset with $n$ elements as a bijection $\omega : P \rightarrow [n]$, and the \emph{order polynomial} $\Omega _{P,\omega}(k)$ as \[ \Omega _{P,\omega} (k) := \# \left\{ (x_1, x_2, ... , x_n) \in [k]^n : \begin{array}{l} x_u \leq x_v \text{ if } u \preceq v \text{ and } \omega (u) < \omega (v) \\ x_u < x_v \text{ if } u \preceq v \text{ and } \omega (u) > \omega (v) \end{array} \right\} . \] (Here $\# S$ denotes the cardinality of the set $S$.)
nodes.section: 2 Posets, Order Polynomials, and the Proof of Theorem 2
nodes.statement_short: An $\omega$-labeling is a bijection $P\to[n]$; $\Omega_{P,\omega}(k)$ counts maps to $[k]$ weakly/strictly order preserving according to the labeling.

nodes.name: Polynomiality of the order polynomial
nodes.statement: Stanley \cite{stanleythesis} proved that $\Omega _{P,\omega}(k)$ is indeed a polynomial in $k$.
nodes.section: 2 Posets, Order Polynomials, and the Proof of Theorem 2

nodes.name: Complementary labeling
nodes.statement: The \emph{complementary labeling} to $\omega$ is the $\overline{\omega}$-labeling of $P$ defined by $\overline{\omega}(v) := n+1-\omega(v)$.
nodes.section: 2 Posets, Order Polynomials, and the Proof of Theorem 2

nodes.name: Order polynomial of the complementary labeling
nodes.statement: Thus \[ \Omega _{P,\overline{\omega}} (k) = \# \left\{ (x_1, x_2, ... , x_n) \in [k]^n : \begin{array}{l} x_u < x_v \text{ if } u \preceq v \text{ and } \omega (u) < \omega (v) \\ x_u \le x_v \text{ if } u \preceq v \text{ and } \omega (u) > \omega (v) \end{array} \right\} . \]
nodes.section: 2 Posets, Order Polynomials, and the Proof of Theorem 2
conclusions: \[ \Omega _{P,\overline{\omega}} (k) = \# \left\{ (x_1, x_2, ... , x_n) \in [k]^n : \begin{array}{l} x_u < x_v \text{ if } u \preceq v \text{ and } \omega (u) < \omega (v) \\ x_u \le x_v \text{ if } u \preceq v \text{ and } \omega (u) > \omega (v) \end{array} \right\} . \]
nodes.statement_short: Under the complementary labeling the weak and strict inequalities of the order polynomial swap roles.

nodes.name: Stanley's reciprocity theorem for order polynomials
nodes.statement: $ \Omega _{P,\omega} (-k) = (-1)^{|P|} \, \Omega_{P,\overline{\omega}} (k) \, . $
nodes.section: 2 Posets, Order Polynomials, and the Proof of Theorem 2
nodes.statement_short: Order polynomials of complementary labelings are reciprocal: $\Omega_{P,\omega}(-k)=(-1)^{|P|}\Omega_{P,\overline\omega}(k)$.
nodes.label: stanley_op

nodes.name: Reciprocity for natural labelings
nodes.statement: The reciprocity relation given in Theorem \ref{stanley_op} takes on a special form when $\omega$ is a \emph{natural labeling} of $P$, i.e., one that respects the order of $P$. (It is easy to see that every poset has a natural labeling.) In this case $\Omega _{P,\omega} (k)$ simply counts all order preserving maps $x: P \to [k]$ (i.e., $u \preceq v \Longrightarrow x_u \le x_v$), whereas $\Omega_{P,\overline{\omega}} (k)$ couns all \emph{strictly} order preserving maps $x: P \to [k]$ (i.e., $u \prec v \Longrightarrow x_u < x_v$). Theorem \ref{stanley_op} implies that these two counting functions are reciprocal.
nodes.section: 2 Posets, Order Polynomials, and the Proof of Theorem 2
nodes.statement_short: For a natural labeling, order-preserving and strictly order-preserving map counts are reciprocal.

nodes.name: Weak chromatic polynomial as a lattice-point count
nodes.statement: For a mixed graph $G=(V,E,A)$ with $n$ vertices, the weak chromatic polynomial $\chi _G(k)$ can be written as \[ \chi _G(k) = \# \left\{ (x_1, x_2, \dots, x_n) \in [k]^n : \begin{array}{l} x_u \leq x_v \text{ if } \vec{uv} \in A \\ x_u \ne x_v \text{ if } uv \in E \end{array} \right\} . \]
nodes.section: 2 Posets, Order Polynomials, and the Proof of Theorem 2
assumptions: For a mixed graph $G=(V,E,A)$ with $n$ vertices
conclusions: the weak chromatic polynomial $\chi _G(k)$ can be written as \[ \chi _G(k) = \# \left\{ (x_1, x_2, \dots, x_n) \in [k]^n : \begin{array}{l} x_u \leq x_v \text{ if } \vec{uv} \in A \\ x_u \ne x_v \text{ if } uv \in E \end{array} \right\} .
nodes.statement_short: $\chi_G(k)$ counts $x\in[k]^n$ with $x_u\le x_v$ on arcs and $x_u\ne x_v$ on edges.

nodes.name: Poset of an acyclic orientation
nodes.statement: Each acyclic orientation of $G$ can be translated into a poset by letting $P = V(G)$ and introducing, for each $u \to v$ in the orientation, the relation $u \preceq v$.
nodes.section: 2 Posets, Order Polynomials, and the Proof of Theorem 2

nodes.name: Orientations $G_1,\ldots,G_m$
nodes.statement: Throughout the remainder of this section, we fix an acyclic mixed graph $G$ and denote by $G_1, G_2, \ldots, G_m$ the (acyclic) orientations of $G$.
nodes.section: 2 Posets, Order Polynomials, and the Proof of Theorem 2

nodes.name: Posets $P_i$ and counts $\phi_{G_i}(k)$
nodes.statement: For each $1 \le i \le m$, denote $P_i$ as the poset created by the orientation $G_i$, and let $\phi_{G_i}(k)$ be the number of weak proper $k$-colorings of $G_i$ that are also weak proper $k$-colorings of $G$.
nodes.section: 2 Posets, Order Polynomials, and the Proof of Theorem 2
nodes.statement_short: $P_i$ is the poset of orientation $G_i$; $\phi_{G_i}(k)$ counts weak proper $k$-colorings of $G_i$ that are weak proper for $G$.

nodes.name: Decomposition of $\chi_G$ over orientations
nodes.statement: If $G$ is an acyclic mixed graph, then $\chi_G(k) = \displaystyle\sum_{i=1}^m \phi_{G_i}(k) \, .$
nodes.section: 2 Posets, Order Polynomials, and the Proof of Theorem 2
nodes.label: phisum

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 4
nodes.statement: It is clear that each weak proper $k$-coloring of $G$ is a weak proper $k$-coloring of $G_i$ for some $1 \le i \le m$. Conversely, assuming $E(G) \ne \varnothing$, for any $1 \le i < j \le k$, there is some $uv \in E(G)$ such that $u \to v$ in $G_i$ and $v \to u$ in $G_j$. This implies that there is no weak proper coloring that is a weak proper $k$-coloring of $G_i$ and~$G_j$. If $E(G) = \varnothing$ then $G$ is the only orientation of itself.
nodes.section: 2 Posets, Order Polynomials, and the Proof of Theorem 2
nodes.statement_short: Every weak proper coloring of $G$ colors some orientation, and two distinct orientations differ on an edge, so the sets are disjoint.

nodes.name: Order-polynomial labeling of an orientation
nodes.statement: For each $G_i$, there exists an $\omega_i$-labeling of $P_i$ such that $$\phi_{G_i}(k) = \Omega_{P_i,\omega_i}(k) \, .$$ Moreover, $\Omega_{P_i,\overline{\omega}_i}(k)$ is the number of $k$-colorings intercompatible with $G_i$.
nodes.section: 2 Posets, Order Polynomials, and the Proof of Theorem 2
conclusions: there exists an $\omega_i$-labeling of $P_i$ such that $$\phi_{G_i}(k) = \Omega_{P_i,\omega_i}(k) \, .$$
$\Omega_{P_i,\overline{\omega}_i}(k)$ is the number of $k$-colorings intercompatible with $G_i$
nodes.statement_short: Each orientation's poset has a labeling whose order polynomial is $\phi_{G_i}$ and whose complement counts intercompatible colorings.
nodes.label: labeling

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 5
nodes.statement: Given the orientation $G_i$, let $R_i$ be the orientation of $G$ obtained by reversing the orientation of the edges in $G_i$ (but not the arcs). We will construct $\omega_i$ recursively. Since $R_i$ is acyclic, there exists a vertex $v \in V$ such that all edges and arcs incident to $v$ are oriented away from it. Set $\omega_i(v) := 1$ and remove $v$ and the arcs incident to $v$. Since $R_i$ is acyclic, $R_i-v$ must also be acyclic. Now repeat, assigning each vertex in the process consecutive $\omega_i$-labels. This gives $\omega_i$-labels that satisfy \[ u \to v \text{ in } R_i \qquad \Longrightarrow \qquad \omega_i(u) < \omega_i(v) \, , \] resulting in an $\omega_i$-labeling of $P_i$, the poset corresponding to $G_i$, that satisfies for $u \preceq v$ \begin{align*} \omega_i(u) < \omega_i(v) \qquad &\Longrightarrow \qquad \vec{uv} \in A(G) \, , \\ \omega_i(u) > \omega_i(v) \qquad &\Longrightarrow \qquad uv \in E(G) \, . \end{align*} So \begin{align*} \Omega_{P_i,\omega_i}(k) &= \# \left\{ (x_1, x_2, ... , x_n) \in [k]^n : \begin{array}{l} x_u \le x_v \text{ if } u \preceq v \text{ and } \omega_i (u) < \omega_i (v) \\ x_u < x_v \text{ if } u \preceq v \text{ and } \omega_i (u) > \omega_i (v) \end{array} \right\} \\ &= \# \left\{ (x_1, x_2, ... , x_n) \in [k]^n : \begin{array}{l} x_u \le x_v \text{ if } u \to v \text{ in } G_i \text{ and } \vec{uv} \in A(G) \\ x_u < x_v \text{ if } u \to v \text{ in } G_i \text{ and } uv \in E(G) \end{array} \right\} \\ &= \phi_{G_i}(k) \, . \end{align*} For the second part of the proof, recall that \begin{align*} \Omega _{P_i,\overline{\omega_i}} (k) &= \# \left\{ (x_1, x_2, ... , x_n) \in [k]^n : \begin{array}{l} x_u < x_v \text{ if } u \preceq v \text{ and } \omega_i (u) < \omega_i (v) \\ x_u \le x_v \text{ if } u \preceq v \text{ and } \omega_i (u) > \omega_i (v) \end{array} \right\} \\ &= \# \left\{ (x_1, x_2, ... , x_n) \in [k]^n : \begin{array}{l} x_u < x_v \text{ if } u \preceq v \text{ and } \vec{uv} \in A(G) \\ x_u \le x_v \text{ if } u \preceq v \text{ and } uv \in E(G) \end{array} \right\} \\ &= \# \text{ colorings intercompatible with } G_i \, . \qedhere \end{align*}
nodes.section: 2 Posets, Order Polynomials, and the Proof of Theorem 2
nodes.statement_short: Construct $\omega_i$ by repeatedly labeling a source of the edge-reversed orientation $R_i$, then compare the defining inequalities.

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 2
nodes.statement: If $G$ is an acyclic mixed graph, then by Lemma \ref{phisum}, \begin{eqnarray*} \chi_G(-k) &=& \displaystyle\sum_{i=1}^m \phi_{G_i}(-k) \\ &=& \displaystyle\sum_{i=1}^m \Omega_{P_i,\omega_i}(-k) \ \text{ (by Lemma \ref{labeling})}\\ &=& \displaystyle\sum_{i=1}^m (-1)^{|P_i|}\Omega_{P_i,\overline{\omega_i}}(k) \ \text{ (by Theorem \ref{stanley_op})}\\ &=& (-1)^{|V|}\displaystyle\sum_{i=1}^m \Omega_{P_i,\overline{\omega_i}}(k) \, . \end{eqnarray*} By applying Lemma \ref{labeling} again, the proof is completed.
nodes.section: 2 Posets, Order Polynomials, and the Proof of Theorem 2
nodes.statement_short: Sum Lemma 4 over orientations, convert each term via Lemma 5 to an order polynomial, and apply Stanley's order-polynomial reciprocity.

nodes.name: Edge and arc deletion
nodes.statement: Let $G=(V,E,A)$ be a mixed graph, $e \in E(G)$, and $a \in A(G)$. Define $G-e = (V,E-e,A)$ as the mixed graph with edge $e$ deleted and $G-a = (V,E,A-a)$ as the mixed graph with arc $a$ deleted.

nodes.name: Contraction of an edge or arc
nodes.statement: An edge or arc is \emph{contracted} by deleting the edge or arc and identifying the vertices incident to it (keeping only one copy of each edge and arc).

nodes.name: Contracted graphs $G/e$, $G/a$
nodes.statement: Denote $G/e$ as the mixed graph obtained by contracting edge $e$ in $G$ and $G/a$ as the mixed graph obtained by contracting arc $a$ in $G$.

nodes.name: Proof of Proposition 6 (standard argument)
nodes.statement: The standard proof for the deletion--contraction formula for (unmixed) graphs gives:
nodes.statement_short: By the standard deletion--contraction argument for unmixed graphs.

nodes.name: Deletion--contraction for edges
nodes.statement: If $G$ is a mixed graph and $e \in E(G)$, then $$\chi_G(k) = \chi_{G-e}(k) - \chi_{G/e}(k) \, .$$
assumptions: $G$ is a mixed graph and $e \in E(G)$
nodes.label: DCedge

nodes.name: Arc reversal $G_a$
nodes.statement: Define $G_{a}$ as the mixed graph $G$ with arc $a$ directed in the reverse direction. In other words, if $a=\vec{uv}$ then $G_{a} = (V,E,A-\{\vec{uv}\} \cup \{\vec{vu}\})$.

nodes.name: Deletion--contraction for arcs
nodes.statement: If $G$ is a mixed graph and $a \in A(G)$, then $$\chi_G(k) + \chi_{G_{a}}(k) = \chi_{G-a}(k) + \chi_{G/a}(k) \, .$$
assumptions: $G$ is a mixed graph and $a \in A(G)$
nodes.label: DCarc

nodes.name: Proof of Proposition 7
nodes.statement: Let $a=\vec{uv}$, $C$ be the set of weak proper $k$-colorings of $G$, and $C_a$ be the set of weak proper $k$-colorings of $G_a$. Therefore, $\chi_G(k) + \chi_{G_{a}}(k) = |C \cup C_a| + |C \cap C_a|$. A coloring $c \in C \cup C_a$ if and only if $c$ is a weak proper $k$-coloring of $G-a$. A coloring $c \in C \cap C_a$ if and only if $c(u) = c(v)$ and $c$ corresponds to a weak proper $k$-coloring of $G/a$ in which the vertex created by identifying $u$ and $v$ is colored with $c(u)$. Therefore, $\chi_{G-a}(k) = |C \cup C_a|$ and $\chi_{G/a}(k) = |C \cap C_a|.$
nodes.statement_short: Inclusion--exclusion on the colorings of $G$ and $G_a$: their union is the colorings of $G-a$, their intersection those of $G/a$.

nodes.name: Deletion--contraction recurrences (1)--(2)
nodes.statement: \chi_G(k) &= \chi_{G-e}(k) - \chi_{G/e}(k) \, , \\ \chi_G(k) &= \chi_{G-a}(k) + \chi_{G/a}(k) - \chi_{G_{a}}(k) \, .
nodes.statement_short: $\chi_G=\chi_{G-e}-\chi_{G/e}$ and $\chi_G=\chi_{G-a}+\chi_{G/a}-\chi_{G_a}$.
nodes.label: dce

nodes.name: Use of the recurrences in computation
nodes.statement: Equation (\ref{dce}) is very useful in computing the weak chromatic polynomials since it recursively gives the weak chromatic polynomial of a mixed graph as a difference of (in the number of vertices or edges) smaller mixed graphs. On the other hand, equation (\ref{dca}) gives the weak chromatic polynomial of $G$ in terms of $G_a$, which is not a smaller graph. However, we will show how it can be used in computation.
nodes.statement_short: Recurrence (1) reduces to smaller graphs; (2) involves $G_a$, which is not smaller, but is still usable.

nodes.name: Strongly connected directed graph
nodes.statement: A directed graph $G=(V,\varnothing, A)$ is \emph{strongly connected} if for any pair of vertices $u,v \in V$ there exists a directed path from $u$ to $v$.
differentia: for any pair of vertices $u,v \in V$ there exists a directed path from $u$ to $v$

nodes.name: Strongly connected digraphs have $\chi_G(k)=k$
nodes.statement: If $G$ is a strongly connected directed graph, then $\chi_G(k) = k$.
assumptions: $G$ is a strongly connected directed graph
nodes.label: cycle_contract_lemma

nodes.name: Proof of Proposition 8
nodes.statement: Fix $u \in V$, and let $c$ be a weak proper coloring of $G$. Since there is a directed path from $u$ to any $v$ and vice versa, $c(v) \le c(u) \le c(v)$ for every $v \in V$. Therefore, $c(u) = c(v)$ for every $v \in V$, and since there are $k$ colors that can be assigned to $u$, $\chi_G(k) = k$.
nodes.statement_short: Directed paths both ways force all vertices to share one color, giving $k$ colorings.

nodes.name: Contraction $G/S$ of a subgraph
nodes.statement: Given a subgraph $S$ of $G$, denote $G/S$ as the mixed graph $G$ with all edges and arcs of $S$ removed and all vertices of $S$ identified to one vertex; resulting parallel edges/arcs should be replaced by a single edge/arc.

nodes.name: Contracting a strongly connected subgraph
nodes.statement: Let $G$ be a mixed graph and $S$ be a strongly connected directed subgraph of $G$. Then $\chi_G(k)=\chi_{G/S}(k)$.
assumptions: Let $G$ be a mixed graph and $S$ be a strongly connected directed subgraph of $G$.
nodes.label: subcontract

nodes.name: Proof of Proposition 9
nodes.statement: Let $s$ be the vertex that $S$ contracts to in $G/S$. For each weak proper $k$-coloring of $G$, the vertices of $S$ must all be colored the same color $j$. By defining $c(s) = j$ we get a bijection between the weak proper $k$-colorings of $G$ and $G/S$.
nodes.statement_short: Vertices of $S$ share a color, giving a bijection between colorings of $G$ and of $G/S$.

nodes.name: Deletion--contraction computation of the weak chromatic polynomial
nodes.statement: Computing the weak chromatic polynomial of a mixed graph is reduced to computing the weak chromatic polynomial of smaller directed graphs by applying Proposition \ref{DCedge}. Computing the weak chromatic polynomial of a directed graph is reduced to computing the weak chromatic polynomial of smaller acyclic directed graphs (directed trees) by recursively reversing arcs and applying Proposition \ref{DCarc} until a strongly connected subgraph is created and Proposition \ref{subcontract} can be applied. Note that a strongly connected subgraph of a directed graph can be obtained by reversing arcs as long as the underlying graph is not acyclic.
nodes.statement_short: Reduce mixed graphs to directed graphs by edge deletion--contraction, then reverse arcs via the arc recurrence until a strongly connected subgraph can be contracted.

nodes.name: Cyclic mixed graph with no intercompatible colorings
nodes.statement: As an example, let $G=(\{u,v,w\}, \{uv\}, \{\vec{vw},\vec{wu} \})$ (shown in Figure \ref{ex1}). $G$ is a cyclic mixed graph since it has an orientation, $G_1$, that contains a directed cycle. Consider $k=2$. If $c$ is an intercompatible coloring of $G_1$ or $G_2$, then $c(v) < c(w) < c(u)$. Therefore, $G_1$ and $G_2$ have no intercompatible colorings and the number of 2-colorings of $G$, each counted with multiplicity equal to the number of intercompatible acyclic orientations of $G$ is~0.
nodes.statement_short: A 3-vertex cyclic mixed graph whose orientations admit no intercompatible 2-colorings, so the reciprocity count is 0.

nodes.name: Weak chromatic polynomial of the cyclic example
nodes.statement: We now use contraction and deletion, with $e=uv$, to compute the weak chromatic polynomial of $G$. The contracted graph $G/e$ (see Figure \ref{ex2}) is a strongly connected directed graph, so $\chi_{G/e}(k) = k$. In $G-e$, there are $(k-i+1)i$ weak proper $k$-colorings with $c(w)=i$. Therefore, \[ \chi_{G-e}(k) = \sum_{i=1}^k (k-i+1)i = \frac{(k+2)(k+1)k}{3} \] and so $\chi_G(k) = \frac 1 3 (k+2)(k+1)k - k$. We can now see that Theorem \ref{main} does not hold for $G$ since $\chi_G(-2) = -2$.
nodes.statement_short: Deletion--contraction gives $\chi_G(k)=\frac13(k+2)(k+1)k-k$, so $\chi_G(-2)=-2\ne0$ and Theorem 2 fails without acyclicity.

nodes.name: Cover and differing edge
nodes.statement: It is clear that each weak proper $k$-coloring of $G$ is a weak proper $k$-coloring of $G_i$ for some $1 \le i \le m$. Conversely, assuming $E(G) \ne \varnothing$, for any $1 \le i < j \le k$, there is some $uv \in E(G)$ such that $u \to v$ in $G_i$ and $v \to u$ in $G_j$.
nodes.section: 2 Posets, Order Polynomials, and the Proof of Theorem 2
nodes.statement_short: Each coloring of $G$ is a coloring of some $G_i$; distinct orientations differ on some edge.

nodes.name: Disjointness
nodes.statement: This implies that there is no weak proper coloring that is a weak proper $k$-coloring of $G_i$ and~$G_j$.
nodes.section: 2 Posets, Order Polynomials, and the Proof of Theorem 2
nodes.statement_short: Hence no coloring is weakly proper for two orientations.

nodes.name: Edgeless case
nodes.statement: If $E(G) = \varnothing$ then $G$ is the only orientation of itself.
nodes.section: 2 Posets, Order Polynomials, and the Proof of Theorem 2
nodes.statement_short: Handle $E(G)=\varnothing$: $G$ is its own unique orientation.

nodes.name: Reverse edges
nodes.statement: Given the orientation $G_i$, let $R_i$ be the orientation of $G$ obtained by reversing the orientation of the edges in $G_i$ (but not the arcs). We will construct $\omega_i$ recursively.
nodes.section: 2 Posets, Order Polynomials, and the Proof of Theorem 2
nodes.statement_short: Introduce $R_i$, $G_i$ with edges reversed, and plan a recursive construction of $\omega_i$.

nodes.name: Recursive labeling
nodes.statement: Since $R_i$ is acyclic, there exists a vertex $v \in V$ such that all edges and arcs incident to $v$ are oriented away from it. Set $\omega_i(v) := 1$ and remove $v$ and the arcs incident to $v$. Since $R_i$ is acyclic, $R_i-v$ must also be acyclic. Now repeat, assigning each vertex in the process consecutive $\omega_i$-labels.
nodes.section: 2 Posets, Order Polynomials, and the Proof of Theorem 2
nodes.statement_short: Repeatedly label a source vertex of the acyclic $R_i$ and delete it.

nodes.name: Labeling property
nodes.statement: This gives $\omega_i$-labels that satisfy \[ u \to v \text{ in } R_i \qquad \Longrightarrow \qquad \omega_i(u) < \omega_i(v) \, , \] resulting in an $\omega_i$-labeling of $P_i$, the poset corresponding to $G_i$, that satisfies for $u \preceq v$ \begin{align*} \omega_i(u) < \omega_i(v) \qquad &\Longrightarrow \qquad \vec{uv} \in A(G) \, , \\ \omega_i(u) > \omega_i(v) \qquad &\Longrightarrow \qquad uv \in E(G) \, . \end{align*}
nodes.section: 2 Posets, Order Polynomials, and the Proof of Theorem 2
nodes.statement_short: Labels increase along $R_i$, so in $P_i$ increasing labels mark arcs and decreasing labels mark edges.

nodes.name: First part
nodes.statement: So \begin{align*} \Omega_{P_i,\omega_i}(k) &= \# \left\{ (x_1, x_2, ... , x_n) \in [k]^n : \begin{array}{l} x_u \le x_v \text{ if } u \preceq v \text{ and } \omega_i (u) < \omega_i (v) \\ x_u < x_v \text{ if } u \preceq v \text{ and } \omega_i (u) > \omega_i (v) \end{array} \right\} \\ &= \# \left\{ (x_1, x_2, ... , x_n) \in [k]^n : \begin{array}{l} x_u \le x_v \text{ if } u \to v \text{ in } G_i \text{ and } \vec{uv} \in A(G) \\ x_u < x_v \text{ if } u \to v \text{ in } G_i \text{ and } uv \in E(G) \end{array} \right\} \\ &= \phi_{G_i}(k) \, . \end{align*}
nodes.section: 2 Posets, Order Polynomials, and the Proof of Theorem 2
nodes.statement_short: Rewrite $\Omega_{P_i,\omega_i}(k)$ as $\phi_{G_i}(k)$.

nodes.name: Second part
nodes.statement: For the second part of the proof, recall that \begin{align*} \Omega _{P_i,\overline{\omega_i}} (k) &= \# \left\{ (x_1, x_2, ... , x_n) \in [k]^n : \begin{array}{l} x_u < x_v \text{ if } u \preceq v \text{ and } \omega_i (u) < \omega_i (v) \\ x_u \le x_v \text{ if } u \preceq v \text{ and } \omega_i (u) > \omega_i (v) \end{array} \right\} \\ &= \# \left\{ (x_1, x_2, ... , x_n) \in [k]^n : \begin{array}{l} x_u < x_v \text{ if } u \preceq v \text{ and } \vec{uv} \in A(G) \\ x_u \le x_v \text{ if } u \preceq v \text{ and } uv \in E(G) \end{array} \right\} \\ &= \# \text{ colorings intercompatible with } G_i \, . \qedhere \end{align*}
nodes.section: 2 Posets, Order Polynomials, and the Proof of Theorem 2
nodes.statement_short: Rewrite $\Omega_{P_i,\overline{\omega_i}}(k)$ as the number of intercompatible colorings.

nodes.name: Inclusion--exclusion setup
nodes.statement: Let $a=\vec{uv}$, $C$ be the set of weak proper $k$-colorings of $G$, and $C_a$ be the set of weak proper $k$-colorings of $G_a$. Therefore, $\chi_G(k) + \chi_{G_{a}}(k) = |C \cup C_a| + |C \cap C_a|$.
nodes.statement_short: Introduce $C$, $C_a$ and write the sum as $|C\cup C_a|+|C\cap C_a|$.

nodes.name: Union
nodes.statement: A coloring $c \in C \cup C_a$ if and only if $c$ is a weak proper $k$-coloring of $G-a$.
nodes.statement_short: Union is the weak proper colorings of $G-a$.

nodes.name: Intersection
nodes.statement: A coloring $c \in C \cap C_a$ if and only if $c(u) = c(v)$ and $c$ corresponds to a weak proper $k$-coloring of $G/a$ in which the vertex created by identifying $u$ and $v$ is colored with $c(u)$.
nodes.statement_short: Intersection corresponds to weak proper colorings of $G/a$.

nodes.name: Conclusion
nodes.statement: Therefore, $\chi_{G-a}(k) = |C \cup C_a|$ and $\chi_{G/a}(k) = |C \cap C_a|.$
nodes.statement_short: Identify both terms.

nodes.name: All colors equal
nodes.statement: Fix $u \in V$, and let $c$ be a weak proper coloring of $G$. Since there is a directed path from $u$ to any $v$ and vice versa, $c(v) \le c(u) \le c(v)$ for every $v \in V$.
nodes.statement_short: Directed paths both ways give $c(v)\le c(u)\le c(v)$.

nodes.name: Count
nodes.statement: Therefore, $c(u) = c(v)$ for every $v \in V$, and since there are $k$ colors that can be assigned to $u$, $\chi_G(k) = k$.
nodes.statement_short: All vertices share a color, so there are $k$ colorings.

nodes.name: Common color on $S$
nodes.statement: Let $s$ be the vertex that $S$ contracts to in $G/S$. For each weak proper $k$-coloring of $G$, the vertices of $S$ must all be colored the same color $j$.
nodes.statement_short: Let $s$ be the contracted vertex; $S$ is monochromatic.

nodes.name: Bijection
nodes.statement: By defining $c(s) = j$ we get a bijection between the weak proper $k$-colorings of $G$ and $G/S$.
nodes.statement_short: Color $s$ by $j$ to get a bijection.

nodes.name: Eliminate edges
nodes.statement: Computing the weak chromatic polynomial of a mixed graph is reduced to computing the weak chromatic polynomial of smaller directed graphs by applying Proposition \ref{DCedge}.
nodes.statement_short: Apply Proposition 6 to reduce to directed graphs.

nodes.name: Reverse arcs
nodes.statement: Computing the weak chromatic polynomial of a directed graph is reduced to computing the weak chromatic polynomial of smaller acyclic directed graphs (directed trees) by recursively reversing arcs and applying Proposition \ref{DCarc}
nodes.statement_short: Recursively reverse arcs, applying Proposition 7.

nodes.name: Contract
nodes.statement: until a strongly connected subgraph is created and Proposition \ref{subcontract} can be applied.
nodes.statement_short: Contract the strongly connected subgraph by Proposition 9.
